leading_positions.synthesis: All six round-1 configurations are a single-part prize on B012 naming the same three laureates: Daniel J. Drucker, Jens Juul Holst and Svetlana Mojsov. Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, who is credited on the ballot entry, is left out in every file. Citation wording differs slightly, from the physiology of GLP-1 and its active form (five files) to establishing GLP-1 as an incretin hormone (Sandberg), but all anchor the prize in hormone physiology and peptide identification, not in a particular drug. What is shared is the merit case: a complete discovery-to-patient chain confirmed in large randomized trials. What is not settled is whether three names can carry the credit, and whether a second part should be added. No member put a second ballot ID into a preferred configuration; second-place alternatives (B024, B009, B046) appear only as alternatives.

areas_of_agreement: B012 is the sole ballot in every member's preferred configuration, with an identical three-name laureate set, and each member says the case rests on the science and not on opening-round unanimity.
Maturity of the GLP-1 work is not questioned by any member: independent randomized outcome trials show benefit in type 2 diabetes and obesity, with cardiovascular and renal benefit now documented.

All six members name the same attribution weaknesses in their own B012 case: Mojsov's contested priority, the absence of Habener and others from the supplied credit list, and the exclusion of Knudsen under the three-person limit.
All six members list B009 among their alternatives; five also list B024 and Wahren-Herlenius lists B046 instead. No member proposes B022 as a primary configuration.

Several members (Perlmann, Sandberg, Linnarsson, Svenningsson, El-Manira) describe Walter and Mori (B024) as a clean two-person attribution; the disagreement concerns weight given to its limited clinical translation.
scientific_disputes: Whether the prize should reward discovery of hormone physiology and the active peptide, or the drug-development step (long-acting agonists) that turned it into medicine. Perlmann and Sandberg regard excluding Knudsen as defensible; Perlmann and Svenningsson also note that protraction chemistry is more than routine translation.

Whether a basic mechanism with largely prospective disease payoff (B024, unfolded protein response) should rank alongside clinically transformative candidates. Sandberg and Perlmann see it as the strongest mechanistic alternative; Wahren-Herlenius and Sandberg stress that its translation is still early.

Whether TNF blockade (B046) is a mechanistic discovery or therapeutic development. Wahren-Herlenius keeps it as an alternative; El-Manira asks whether the decisive step was showing TNF drives synovial inflammation or clinical proof of concept.

Whether BCR-ABL targeted therapy (B016) is a class-defining paradigm or essentially one drug in one disease, as argued in several responses to the chair, and whether it is maturely recognised without the oncogene biology.
attribution_disputes: B012: Mojsov's priority for identifying GLP-1(7-36) is contested relative to Habener and colleagues, who are absent from the supplied credit list. No member can verify the priority history from the files.

B012: Knudsen is credited on the ballot but excluded by all six. Members disagree on how openly the citation must acknowledge that omission, and Perlmann would not accept a configuration that includes Knudsen at the expense of the basic-science names.

B009: Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept lies outside the credited names. Linnarsson, Sandberg, Perlmann and Wahren-Herlenius question including Rosenberg, whose adoptive cell transfer is seen as a distinct strand; Wahren-Herlenius says she has moved toward the two-name (June, Sadelain) version, which still leaves Eshhar unresolved.

B016: the BCR-ABL oncogene discovery (Rowley, Witte, Konopka and others) and the Ciba-Geigy chemistry sit outside the credited trio, so the entry would credit drug development while leaving target discovery to others.
B022: six credited names, a disputed split between channelrhodopsin discovery and neuronal deployment, and earlier fly work by Miesenbock mean that any trio omits a decisive contributor.
maturity_disputes: B009 (CAR-T): Linnarsson and Perlmann cite open questions on durability, secondary malignancy and solid tumours, and treat it as an alternative and not a co-equal second part; Wahren-Herlenius says TNF blockade has more than twenty years of independent confirmation by comparison.
B024: no dispute on scientific confirmation, but Sandberg and Wahren-Herlenius question whether clinical relevance is mature enough to carry a prize on its own.
B012: no maturity dispute; Perlmann notes only that obesity indications and long-term safety data are still evolving.
B022: Sandberg and Perlmann describe medical application as limited to first vision-restoration uses, against very large experimental impact.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Svenningsson (chair) discloses about twenty co-authored works with Perlmann on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy; Perlmann discloses the same co-authorship. Neither reports any shortlisted credited name as a collaborator, and neither finds a recusal-level conflict.

El-Manira discloses a 2009 paper with Perlmann and with Ernfors and a shared lamprey model system with Grillner, none credited on the shortlist, and notes that he uses optogenetics (B022) as a tool, which he describes as a subject interest and not a personal connection.

Linnarsson discloses co-authorship with Sandberg and a 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper, neither connected to a shortlisted candidate; Sandberg discloses co-authorship with Linnarsson and Frisen and shared institutional affiliation with colleagues.
Perlmann also discloses prior working connections to Ronald Evans and Johan Ericson, neither on the shortlist.

Wahren-Herlenius notes that her field (autoimmunity and rheumatology) is close to B046 (TNF blockade), with no documented connection to Feldmann or Maini, and says she would recuse if a connection were identified.
questions_for_round2: Should the B012 citation be worded around the physiology and active form of GLP-1 only, and if so, what wording openly states that the development of long-acting agonists (Knudsen) is not what the prize rewards?

Can the committee settle Mojsov's standing relative to Habener and others from evidence available to it, and if not, is a configuration with Mojsov still defensible, or should a different third name be considered?

Should the prize be a single GLP-1 part, or should a second distinct achievement share it? If a second part, which ballot (B024, B009 or B046) and which exact names, given that Eshhar, Rosenberg and the PERK arm are all contested?
For B009, does a two-name June and Sadelain configuration resolve enough of the Eshhar and Rosenberg questions to move it from alternative to a candidate second part?
For B024, does the absence of translation to patients count against the prize this year, or is a clean two-person mechanistic discovery an adequate second part alongside a clinical one?
For B016 and B046, is the deciding element the target biology or the drug and clinical proof of concept, and does that make either a candidate for this year or a later one?
summary.chair_observation: The six round-1 files agree on one configuration and on the same weaknesses in it, so round 2 does not need to choose a leader. It needs to test the stated weaknesses: Knudsen's exclusion, Mojsov versus Habener, and whether a second part is warranted. Agreement on B012 is explicit in all six configurations, while the ordering of alternatives is not yet reconciled and is stated in different ways across the files.
